raw_response:
I'm 57 this year, been farming these 2.6 mu in Quzhou since I was a teenager. Never went to school — my mother taught me everything in the fields. It's just me and my old man at home now, so we can't manage much land. I grow chili on the whole plot. I tried wheat and corn years ago, but on a small piece like this, chili brings better money, and I've been doing it long enough that I know the buyers and the rhythm.

I bought my chili seedlings from the county market in late April, the same improved variety with thick flesh that I've used for years. The seedlings cost me about 130 yuan per mu. Me and my old man ran the small walking tractor over the field once, then leveled it by hand with hoes. We planted the seedlings by hand — took us three days of bending over, just the two of us.

For fertilizer, I spread two bags of that compound fertilizer — the 15-15-15 kind — across the whole field before planting. My neighbor Lao Zhang does the same and his chilies always look strong. Then when the first flowers show in June, I topdress with most of a bag of urea and a small bag of potassium fertilizer. I don't weigh it in kilos — I know my 2.6 mu needs two bags of compound for the base, and about thirty or forty jin of urea later. The soil here is decent.

I have my well, but the pump eats electricity, so I water carefully. I irrigate well when we transplant the seedlings, then again at flowering time, and once more in July if the drought comes. Three times is enough for a normal year. Every time I turn on that pump I watch the cost, so I don't waste water.

Pests always come — aphids and that wilt that turns the leaves yellow. I spray three or four times through the season with whatever the agricultural supply shop recommends. Usually an insecticide and a fungicide mixed in the tank. I don't read those labels myself — the shop man knows my field and tells me what to buy.

For labor, it's almost all me and my old man. We might hire someone for three or four days in August and September when the chilies need picking every few days and there's too many for us to handle. Hired hands want 100 yuan a day now, which is too much, so we only do it if we're desperate.

I hope to get about six hundred jin of dried chilies per mu this year if the weather holds — that's about what I got last year. I don't spend too much on inputs because if the market price drops, I'm stuck. My total spending on seedlings, fertilizer, pesticide, water, and some hired help will be about 1,800 yuan. That's a big piece of our savings, but we have to spend money to make money.
